clue.text: Advanced showing with VIP? We're excited

indicators.note: excited letters are stirred up, so the letters of VIP and we're are jumbled together

parts.note: the contraction contributes its four letters, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A celebrity is invited to an early screening and the staff are thrilled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' rearranges VIPWERE. A nod to the theme: Eric Morecambe famously called the conductor André Previn 'Mr Preview'.
explanation.definitionFit: A screening held in advance of the public release is a sneak showing of that kind.

clue.text: Place with facility to gratify

parts.note: PL is the abbreviation for Place in addresses
ease means facility, doing something effortlessly

explanation.surface: A venue with good amenities that aims to satisfy guests.
explanation.definitionFit: To gratify someone is to give them satisfaction or delight.

clue.text: Beaten one nil when weather is changeable

indicators.note: beaten letters are knocked about, so one and nil are rearranged

explanation.surface: A team loses one-nil in unsettled conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beaten' looks like a football result word but rearranges ONENIL.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pacific warming phenomenon brings periods of disrupted climate patterns worldwide.

clue.text: When corrupted, "goodies" lie to obtain convictions

indicators.note: corrupted letters are spoilt and disordered, so goodies and lie are rearranged

explanation.surface: Good guys gone bad tell lies to win their cause.
explanation.definitionFit: Systems of belief are firmly held principles or convictions.

clue.text: Women's Institute meeting politicians in big girls' blouses

parts.note: WI is the Women's Institute, a British community organisation for women
MPs are Members of Parliament

explanation.surface: The Women's Institute meeting MPs who turn out to be feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meeting' joins the two pieces. A 'big girl's blouse' is British slang for a weak, timid man, a phrase popularised in a 1960s sitcom.
explanation.definitionFit: Big girls' blouses is British slang for feeble, cowardly men.

clue.text: It's surrounded by columns of men in exercise with one commander

indicators.note: the word in places the men inside the exercise abbreviation

parts.note: PT is physical training
OR, other ranks, is the military abbreviation for ordinary soldiers
the Roman numeral for one
CO is a commanding officer

explanation.surface: A drill session for troops under a single officer, described in barracks language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals the container. 'men' in crosswords is often the army's other ranks, and the definition describes a pillared porch.
explanation.definitionFit: A porch or entrance with a roof held up by a row of pillars fits the description of being ringed with columns.

clue.text: Shark almost left at sea by Darwin's ship

indicators.note: almost the whole word, losing its final letter

parts.note: on a ship, port is the left side
HMS Beagle carried Charles Darwin on his voyage

explanation.surface: A shark is nearly abandoned in the ocean by Darwin's vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims PORT to POR.
explanation.definitionFit: The porbeagle is a species of mackerel shark of the North Atlantic.

clue.text: In reverse, people-carrier carries people

indicators.note: in reverse means the letters are read backwards
the phrase carries the run of letters within it

explanation.surface: A minivan in reverse gear transports passengers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carries' finds ECAR inside people-carrier, and 'In reverse' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A race is a people or ethnic group.

clue.text: It's memorable how Castor distinguished himself from Pollux

definitions.text: how Castor distinguished himself from Pollux

explanation.surface: A classical riddle about the famous twins.
explanation.walkthrough: In myth Castor was mortal and his twin Pollux immortal, so Castor might say 'I'm mortal'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something everlasting in fame will always be remembered; and split as I'M MORTAL it is the mortal twin's self-description.

clue.text: Admiral's position relative to Captain Burn

parts.note: an admiral outranks a captain, so is over him
Captain James Cook, the explorer

explanation.surface: Asking how an admiral ranks against a captain named Burn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Captain Burn' reads as a name; 'Captain' gives COOK and 'Burn' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To spoil food by leaving it on the heat too long is to burn it.

clue.text: Man of note seen diving into lake

indicators.note: something diving into a body of water goes inside it, so one piece is placed within the lake

parts.note: Lake Erie, one of the North American Great Lakes
n is a standard abbreviation for note, as in footnote references

explanation.surface: A famous musician is spotted plunging into a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man of note' looks like the definition, but 'of note' must supply the N: the definition is just 'Man', here Ernie Wise, the theme's straight man.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernie is a man's first name, as borne by Ernie Wise of the comedy double act.

clue.text: Reinforcements arrived to capture British town

parts.note: reinforcements are more troops

indicators.note: capturing something means holding it inside, so the British letter goes within the phrase

parts.note: came means arrived

explanation.surface: Extra troops turn up and take a town in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to capture' puts B inside MORECAME, just before the final E. Morecambe is a seaside town in Lancashire, from which Eric Morecambe took his stage name.
explanation.definitionFit: Morecambe is a resort community on the Lancashire coast of England.

clue.text: Police business involves breaking Susan's legs?

indicators.note: breaking the words up lets their letters be reassembled in a new order

parts.note: the possessive s here is a real letter of the fodder

explanation.surface: Officers investigating a nasty assault on a woman called Susan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' rearranges SUSANSLEGS. The question mark flags a whimsical definition: dark glasses are the stereotyped kit of the police officer, and glasses also have legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinted glasses are a stock part of the traffic cop's image, so wearing them is part of the job.

clue.text: What are the rich mostly? Idle?

indicators.note: most of the letters of the rich are kept, losing only the outer ones, leaving a name

explanation.surface: A jibe asking whether wealthy people are generally lazy.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop TH and the final H from THERICH. 'Idle?' is a definition by example: Eric Idle of Monty Python, and also the forename of Eric Morecambe.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric is the first name of the Python comic surnamed Idle, the query marking a definition by example.

clue.text: So what? To Dad, just turning up is ideal …

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
eh is a query meaning what
taken as written
pa means dad

explanation.surface: A shrug to a father who simply arriving counts as perfection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' reverses SOEHTOPA to APOTHEOS; IS follows. 'just' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An apotheosis is the perfect example, the highest point or ideal of something.

clue.text: Iconic arpeggio I changed for right notes … but not necessarily in the right order

definitions.text: Iconic arpeggio I changed for right notes … but not necessarily in the right order

indicators.text: but not necessarily in the right order
indicators.note: letters not in their proper order are scrambled, so the whole pool is rearranged
one letter is swapped out and replaced by the following pieces

parts.note: the letter I, one of the three in the first words
taken as written

explanation.surface: A famous piano run gets fiddled with, the notes all correct but jumbled.
explanation.walkthrough: In ICONICARPEGGIO, 'changed for' swaps one I for R and NOTES; the anagram indicator rearranges the result. The whole clue recalls Eric Morecambe's line to André Previn: 'I'm playing all the right notes, but not necessarily in the right order.'
explanation.definitionFit: The Norwegian composer's keyboard showpiece is the work Eric mangled in the famous Previn sketch.

clue.text: … to see you take wedding vow before worshippers

indicators.note: before places the vow ahead of the farewell

parts.note: I do is the vow said at a wedding
laters is slang for see you later

explanation.surface: Saying goodbye before marrying among the congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from 13 Down. 'I do' comes before LATERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Idolaters are those who worship images or false gods.

clue.text: See 14 Across
One undressing a good man's very good down under!

parts.note: ST, saint, is a good man
ripper is Australian slang for something excellent

explanation.surface: An Australian praising a fine man who is taking his clothes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down under' means Australia. 'The Stripper' was the music for a famous Morecambe and Wise breakfast sketch.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer who removes clothes for an audience is someone undressing.

clue.text: Entering frequently those people sign in

indicators.note: pieces entering another go inside it, so two words sit within the adverb

parts.note: oft is an old word for frequently
them means those people
an omen is a sign

explanation.surface: Regularly, some people turn up and sign the register.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entering' signals the container. The one-word definition 'in' is easy to read as a link word; here it means fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in is currently fashionable, the same as being trendy right now.

clue.text: Rosie Brewer's a bird with a heart of gold

indicators.note: something forming the heart sits in the middle, so gold goes inside the bird

parts.note: a tern is a seabird
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A woman named Rosie Brewer is a kind-hearted lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosie Lee is Cockney rhyming slang for tea, so a 'Rosie brewer' makes tea. 'bird' looks like slang for a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A large metal vessel for making tea in quantity is a tea-brewer, Rosie being rhyming slang for that drink.

clue.text: Like Schoenberg composition, note, getting no thanks in return

indicators.note: in return means the whole run of letters is read backwards

parts.note: la is a note of the sol-fa scale
taken as written
ta is British informal for thanks

explanation.surface: A Schoenberg piece that earned no gratitude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in return' reverses LANOTA.
explanation.definitionFit: Schoenberg wrote music without a key centre, the defining feature of that style.

clue.text: Tony Curtis's leading part here in Rome

indicators.note: the leading part of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: hic is Latin, the language of ancient Rome, for here

explanation.surface: The film star Tony Curtis plays the lead in a Roman epic.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Curtis appeared in Roman films, but 'Tony' is the definition: tony means stylish.
explanation.definitionFit: Tony is an informal adjective for high-class and stylish.

clue.text: Birth of one out of seven little ones reaching seventy without extremities

parts.words: one out of seven little ones
parts.note: Happy is one of the Seven Dwarfs in the Snow White story

indicators.note: a word without its extremities loses its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A septuagenarian receives news of the arrival of a baby, one of seven.
explanation.walkthrough: Seventy without its first and last letters gives EVENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A happy event is a euphemistic idiom for the arrival of a baby.

clue.text: Where to find most of the alphabet spaghetti perhaps

definitions.text: Where to find most of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A riddle about alphabet spaghetti.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as PAST A: every letter but the first comes after A.
explanation.definitionFit: All letters but one come after the first letter; and spaghetti is an example of Italian noodles.

clue.text: Canny-y-y-y, as one might say

indicators.note: said aloud, the run of letters is heard as a word

parts.note: a string of Ys, said aloud

explanation.surface: Someone drawing out the word canny in a long northern drawl.
explanation.walkthrough: Several Ys, spoken, sound like 'whys'. Ernie Wise is the theme's other half.
explanation.definitionFit: Canny means shrewd and sensible, which is sagacious.

clue.text: They fix cloth on clothes horses

parts.note: rep is a ribbed woven fabric
airers are frames for drying laundry

explanation.surface: Fabric draped over drying racks.
explanation.definitionFit: People who mend broken things are menders, those who fix.

clue.text: Say no to egg on muffin in the end

parts.note: to spur is to urge or egg on

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: Turning down a breakfast muffin with egg on it.
explanation.definitionFit: To reject or refuse something scornfully is to say no to it.

clue.text: Unable to paddle in old French city seaside centre

parts.note: Arles is a city in Provence, southern France

indicators.note: the centre of a seven-letter word is its fourth letter

explanation.surface: Someone at a beach resort in an old French city finds they cannot go in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paddle' suggests wading at the seaside, but it means rowing: a boat without blades cannot be paddled.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking any rowing blades, a boat cannot be propelled by the crew.

clue.text: One learns about a team

parts.note: A means one, as in a single item

indicators.note: about signals the letters of learns being moved around

explanation.surface: Someone studies a sports side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' signals the anagram of LEARNS, giving RSENAL; 'One' reads as a pronoun but supplies the opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenal is a London football club, an example of a sports side.
